talks.title: API's Dark Side: Addressing AppSec's Biggest Challenge
talks.teaser: Explains the OWASP API Security Top 10 risks, with access control singled out as the hardest problem to get right.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the shift in how modern applications are built. Clients now exchange raw JSON with servers that act mainly as data proxies, and the logic runs in the client. Every endpoint adds to the attack surface, and APIs are easy to spin up, so forgotten or undocumented ones often remain exposed. The speaker argues that classic flaws such as SQL injection are becoming less common, while API-specific weaknesses are growing.

The middle of the talk walks through the OWASP API Security Top 10, which the speaker helped create. Broken authentication comes from missing protections such as brute-force defenses, or from weak implementations like misused JWTs and unsalted passwords. Broken object-level and function-level authorization are presented as the core access control failures, with examples of users reaching other users' objects or calling admin functions. Excessive data exposure happens when apps filter sensitive fields on the client instead of the server, and a dating app case showed hidden fields leaking. Mass assignment lets an attacker set privileged properties such as a role. The remaining categories cover missing rate limits, security misconfiguration, and improper asset management, including legacy or beta API versions that were never documented or protected.

The closing message is that access control is the central challenge and must be designed in from the start. Practitioners should keep an inventory of APIs, document them, and retire unused versions, and they should scrutinize third-party APIs as carefully as open-source dependencies. The speaker also noted that the list is being updated to cover formats such as GraphQL.

talks.title: Container Scanning: Run Fast and Stay Safe
talks.teaser: Shows where container image scanning fits in a build pipeline, registry and Kubernetes admission webhooks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common gap: Kubernetes and Docker keep workloads running but do little to protect the software packaged inside each container. The presenter argues that containers are short-lived, identical each time they start, and rarely change in place, so a container's installed software can be inventoried once and checked against a vulnerability database. Container scanning is presented as one input alongside unit tests, static analysis and license checks, feeding a go or no-go decision mapped to organizational policy.

The middle of the talk covers when to scan. Options include the build pipeline, the container registry, Kubernetes validating admission webhooks at pod launch, and running clusters. A new image can take around ten minutes to inventory, while a result cached by image hash returns almost immediately. The presenter demonstrates Anchore, an open-source scanner that runs as microservices, through its command-line tool and a GitHub Actions workflow. The demo covers building a package inventory with licenses, comparing it to vulnerability feeds, and applying a policy that fails the build. Limitations were noted: feed downloads can be slow, and the scanner reads package manifests rather than every file on disk.

The closing section stresses that the failure threshold is an organizational decision. Teams must decide how much risk to tolerate when no fix exists and whether a vulnerable service should be blocked or kept running. Suggested practices include rebuilding images on a schedule, letting operations trigger rebuilds without developer involvement, and running tests in multi-stage Dockerfiles so that failing tests stop an image before it reaches the registry.

talks.title: Level Up Your Vulnerability Management Program
talks.teaser: Shows how to tie vulnerability scanning to patching, asset context and risk prioritization after a scanner rollout stalls.
talks.summary:
Andy Jordan opens by observing that many organizations stop at deploying a vulnerability scanner. He names three recurring causes: scanner results that conflict with patch reports, little guidance for prioritizing a growing backlog, and manual processes with no clear path to automation. He frames vulnerability management as a lifecycle shared by security and IT, contrasting the security view with the IT patch cycle of staging, deployment and validation.

The middle of the talk covers practical setup in Nessus Pro, including default scan types, the value of authenticated scanning and tuning of concurrency settings. A lab test of different concurrency levels showed modest network and CPU impact and little memory change, so scanner sizing can rest on measurement rather than assumption. For missing asset inventories, he suggests building a working list from existing scan, endpoint and directory data, then adding application, exposure and logging context. He compares binary, NIST SP 800-30 and FAIR risk models, and recommends tracking findings by vulnerability and platform along with closure times. He cautions against pushing raw scan output straight into ticketing and proposes a few orchestration triggers, such as critical findings on mission-critical systems or exploitable externally facing hosts.

He closes with a scenario showing how a report enriched with asset context and root-cause fixes changes the conversation with IT. In the questions he discusses agent-based versus network scanning, preferring agents with network scanners as a backup, and the difficulty of assigning ownership for cloud assets.

talks.title: Dissecting the Ransomware Kill Chain: Why Companies Need It
talks.teaser: Presents a 15-step ransomware kill chain and practical advice for building response plans around extortion and data theft.
talks.summary:
Kurtis Minder and Bryce Webster-Jacobsen of GroupSense open by arguing that ransomware does not fit neatly into traditional attack frameworks such as the Lockheed Martin kill chain. They describe a market where access is bought and sold, cryptocurrency makes large payments easy, and attackers often rely on simple weaknesses like exposed remote access, weak passwords and missing multi-factor authentication.

The core of the talk is a 15-step ransomware kill chain running from first access through encryption. The speakers walk through targeting, noting that some groups avoid certain regions or industries while others pursue large-revenue firms, and that attackers often follow up on successes within a sector. Later stages cover privilege escalation, searching for financial, HR and legal records that can serve as leverage, and stealing data before encryption. They point out that the most practical places to disrupt an attack are early, when access is offered for sale, and at command-and-control, though detection there often comes too late.

Beyond the network, they describe a blast radius that reaches morale, customers, public relations, legal notifications and cyber insurance. Practical guidance includes not rebooting machines or searching for quick decryptors, avoiding contact with extortionists until ready, involving legal counsel and PR early, and reading insurance terms before an incident. They also stress checking sanctions exposure and note that backups do not remove extortion risk or re-intrusion. The takeaway is to test incident response and continuity plans, keep a printed copy, and include non-technical stakeholders.
